segments.title: Build quality and class variation
segments.body: Warships are not assembly-line products. Even nominal sister ships can leave a yard with bulkheads a few inches from their intended positions or different steel fitted. On older ships, builders sometimes compensated for a misplaced bulkhead with thicker steel instead of moving it. A later engine variant can also be slightly heavier or lighter than the unit originally specified. A hundred-ton difference in a 10,000-ton design is only one percent, yet many modest substitutions can accumulate into tens or hundreds of tons across a large vessel. Trials establish how the ship that was actually built compares with its design and with the rest of its class.

evidence.note: Same-class ships varying through steel choice, bulkhead placement, yard practice, and construction decisions.
Engine variants and many small system changes are described as accumulating into tens or hundreds of tons.

segments.summary: Small differences in bulkhead placement, steel, machinery, and weight explain why sister ships still need individual trials.

segments.title: Range, efficiency, and metacentric height
segments.body: Speed trials measure more than maximum knots. Fuel efficiency determines practical range, and an engine revision can raise power while reducing efficiency. These differences also affect whether ships can operate together. Maneuvering trials test the completed ship's stability, including how its metacentric height affects rolling and heeling during high-energy turns. Together, the tests show whether changes in machinery and weight have altered the performance expected from the design.

evidence.note: The transcript explains that efficiency determines range and that an engine change can trade fuel economy for greater power and top speed.
Maneuvering trials are said to reveal the ship's metacentric height and its response to high-energy maneuvers.

segments.summary: Speed and maneuvering trials turn design estimates into measured range, fuel efficiency, and stability under high-energy turns.

segments.title: Fixed versus moving shock trials
segments.body: A ship and an explosive charge can be fixed at known positions to produce controlled shock-trial data. A warship in combat will normally be moving, introducing a relatively small variation in the angle and effect of the shock. The controlled test supplies a reliable baseline, while an underway test adds the variation caused by motion. Both are useful, although shock testing deliberately stresses and can damage a new ship. Builders and governments face repair costs and commissioning delays, making fixed trials an economically attractive choice.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts clean stationary-trial data with the variable shock angles and effects created by a moving ship.
Shock trials are described as damage-producing tests that can delay service and impose repair costs on builders and governments.

segments.summary: Stationary shock trials give controlled data, while trials underway introduce the small variations in shock effects caused by a moving ship.

segments.title: Vibration and unexpected system interference
segments.body: Shore tests cannot reproduce every interaction found in a complete warship. Equipment can function correctly on land and begin to conflict after another shipboard system introduces vibration through the hull. Early radar sets were particularly vulnerable to false positives caused by interactions that designers had not expected. The source could be a generator rather than the main engines, with imperfect bearings creating small vibrations that reached equipment in the superstructure. Sea trials reveal these installation-specific effects because they test the systems together inside the real structure.

evidence.note: Systems passing shore tests and then interacting through vibration after installation at sea.
Early-radar false positives are linked to generator bearings and vibration transmitted from the hull into the superstructure.

segments.summary: Generators and hull vibration can cause false radar returns even when the equipment worked correctly during shore testing.

segments.title: Refit testbeds reduce risk for future warship classes
segments.body: Weapons and sensors must be proved before a costly warship is exposed to combat. One way to reduce development risk is to install next-generation equipment in a current ship during refit and learn from its exercises and operations. Type 23 frigate upgrades have tested systems intended for the Type 26 program, giving maintainers and operators practical experience before the new class enters service. Sea Ceptor installations on Type 45 destroyers offer another way to bring equipment into service and check its integration. This approach moves part of the development risk away from the commissioning schedule of the future ship.

evidence.note: The transcript connects weapons proof and operational exercises with the need to test a warship's fitted systems.
Type 23 testing for Type 26 systems and Sea Ceptor installation on Type 45s are presented as development de-risking.

segments.summary: The Royal Navy's refit strategy shows how next-generation weapons and combat systems can be debugged on serving ships before a new class depends on them.

segments.title: Software updates can disrupt integrated ship systems
segments.body: Trials cannot eliminate every error in installation or operation, and later upgrades can introduce fresh faults. A routine software update can disrupt an interface even when neither the update nor the affected application is malicious. On a warship, the consequences include whether navigation computers, missile systems, and other equipment can still exchange data correctly. Modern ships combine extensive computing and data storage with propulsion, electrical power, accommodation, and weapons. Testing must establish how these systems work together after changes.

evidence.note: A routine computer update illustrates installation, operating, and software-interface failures affecting navigation, missiles, and data exchange.
Modern ships combine computing and data handling with power generation, propulsion, personnel support, and weapons.

segments.summary: Navigation, weapons, and data networks depend on interfaces that can fail after an otherwise ordinary software update.

segments.title: Why new ships need sailors before commissioning
segments.body: HMS Queen Elizabeth was ordered in 2008, laid down in 2009, launched in 2014, and commissioned in 2017. A nine-person advance crew was already assigned before the senior officer who served from 2012 to 2016 arrived. By his departure, the assigned crew had grown to 580 personnel. Those sailors were testing systems and discussing how the ship would operate while construction continued. Their involvement explains why a new ship draws on personnel before entering the operational fleet.

evidence.note: Queen Elizabeth construction dates and an assigned crew growing from nine to 580 establish the personnel commitment before commissioning.
The reported audience question asks where the sailors are and why new ships strain personnel numbers, answered by sailors already testing systems during construction.

segments.summary: Queen Elizabeth's construction crew explains the personnel commitment required years before a new warship enters service.
segments.question: Why do new warships put pressure on sailor numbers before they enter service?
segments.answerShort: Sailors are assigned during construction to test equipment and help resolve operating problems years before commissioning.

segments.title: Command-station chairs affect safety and alertness
segments.body: A command-station chair must support its occupant through shock and allow access to the controls and a quick exit in an emergency. Ordinary wheeled chairs can roll dangerously when a ship heels, so the seat needs to stay fixed in position, although it may swivel. Some stations are occupied around the clock whenever the ship is at sea. An uncomfortable chair or badly arranged working position makes each watch harder and can reduce the operator's alertness. Crew involvement helps test these practical requirements before the layout becomes permanent.

evidence.note: Command-center seating must support occupants under shock, allow access and emergency escape, and remain fixed when a ship heels.
Continuously occupied stations make seating comfort and position important to crew fatigue and alertness.

segments.summary: Seating trials check whether sailors can remain supported, reach their controls, escape quickly, and stay alert through long watches.

segments.title: Crew access checks change Type 45 firefighting arrangements
segments.body: Maintenance procedures depend on whether sailors can physically reach the equipment. During Type 45 construction, crew members found firefighting gear positioned behind steps and a door. Its location looked acceptable on a drawing, but the obstacles delayed access from the routes damage-control personnel would actually use. Crew complaints led to a change while the ship was still being built. Similar decisions matter on carriers expected to serve for about 40 years, because rebuilding command spaces, bridges, or internal routes later is expensive.

evidence.note: Maintenance access and a Type 45 firefighting-gear location behind steps and a door show why actual crew routes matter.
Early crew involvement allows layout changes before a carrier begins an expected 40-year service life and major internal rebuilding becomes expensive.

segments.summary: Type 45 sailors identified obstacles between damage-control teams and their firefighting gear, allowing the layout to be corrected during construction.

segments.title: Type 23 life extension and the frigate gap
segments.body: Visible framing through Type 23 hull plating shows the accumulated effect of the sea on a lightly built frigate. That wear is not necessarily an original build-quality failure, because the class remained in service longer than its early assumptions anticipated. Life extension required replacing plating and other worn structure. Repeated decisions to defer a replacement frigate program eventually created pressure on fleet numbers even when the old design was sound.

evidence.note: The transcript explains Type 23 light framing, ocean-induced plating deformation, life extension, and delayed replacement decisions.

segments.summary: Visible Type 23 hull wear becomes a lesson in the difference between poor construction and extending a lightly built frigate beyond its intended service life.

segments.title: Sea trials expose loose data connections
segments.body: A warship's many computers depend on a large number of cables and connections. A connector that appears secure during installation can fail to make proper contact or work loose in service. Hull vibration, engine operation, ship movement, and repeated heating and cooling all test the installation. Trials aim to expose those faults before the ship deploys. Finding a defect does not by itself establish fault on someone's part, because small connection problems can be difficult to eliminate across so many systems.

evidence.note: Build-quality checks must cover electronics and the many data-cable connections aboard a ship, without assuming every fault establishes blame.
Vibration, machinery, movement, and temperature cycles can loosen connections and expose problems at sea.

segments.summary: Vibration, movement, and temperature cycles can turn an apparently secure cable connection into an operational fault.

segments.title: Speed trials and commissioning politics
segments.body: Seydlitz reached 28 knots on trials but normally operated closer to 26.5 knots, illustrating why the headline number needs its test conditions. German ships tended to be commissioned before trials, while British commissioning followed successful trials and acceptance that the ship worked. German vessels could be tried before they were fully stocked, producing impressive performance figures during an intense naval race. Those results helped the navy advertise capability while limiting pressure for expensive qualitative competition and budget disputes with the army. A commissioned naval crew also followed different safety criteria and could push machinery differently from a civilian trials crew. Loading and crew status therefore affect comparisons between published trial figures.

evidence.note: British and German commissioning practices are contrasted, and incomplete loading explains higher trial speeds.
Naval-race headlines, German budget politics, Seydlitz operational speed, and civilian-versus-naval trial crews affect comparisons.

segments.summary: Seydlitz and contrasting British-German practice show how loading, crew status, naval competition, and budget politics shape reported trial performance.

segments.title: Hull shape determines cruising efficiency
segments.body: Speed and efficiency trials help establish whether sister ships perform alike and whether a hull has been built to the intended shape. A poorly shaped hull can lose substantial cruising efficiency even when its installed machinery provides the expected power. That changes the relationship between economical speed and the much greater power needed for maximum speed. Laser measurements can reveal construction deviations ashore, but water pressure can make the completed hull behave differently once afloat. Trials remain necessary even when the hull has passed detailed geometric inspection.

evidence.note: Hull shaping affects cruising efficiency and the relationship between economical operation and full-power speed.
Laser measurements ashore do not eliminate the need to test a completed hull under water pressure.

segments.summary: A hull can have the expected machinery power and still consume too much fuel because its shape creates excessive cruising resistance.

segments.title: Maneuvering tests and survivability
segments.body: Maneuvering trials give the hull, steering gear, and machinery a different workout from constant-speed endurance tests. World War I submarine experience made zigzagging a major practice in World War II, intended to disrupt an attacker's ranging and firing position. Crash stops and rapid speed changes impose their own loads. High speed also provides strategic dash capability and makes a ship a more difficult target as it enters battle. Against aircraft, torpedoes, or missiles, erratic movement can improve the chance that a decoy succeeds even when it cannot guarantee survival. These trials also expose internal failures: one British carrier revealed a problem in a system intended to drain aviation fuel lines back to protected tanks.

evidence.note: The transcript connects wartime zigzagging with steering, crash stops, speed changes, and machinery stress in maneuvering trials.
High-speed movement, erratic maneuvers, decoys, bombing, torpedoes, and missiles are linked to a warship's last-ditch survivability.
Maneuvering exposing a British carrier problem in a system that drained aviation fuel lines.

segments.summary: Zigzagging, crash stops, decoy use, and a carrier fuel-system problem show why a warship must be tested beyond steady-speed runs.

segments.title: Machinery shock and quieting checks
segments.body: HMAS Diamantina's triple-expansion machinery demonstrates that an older steam plant is simple only in comparison with still more complicated machinery. Its bearings and interacting components can be misbuilt or disturbed by maneuver and explosive shock. A long production run lets experienced inspectors recognize what looks wrong, but most modern warship classes are too small for that familiarity to replace trials. A damaged computer shows how an impact can propagate beyond the visibly struck component into electronics elsewhere in a system. Machinery and computers are therefore mounted or rafted to absorb vibration, and testing must confirm that the isolators have not locked solid. Effective rafting supports both shock survival and acoustic quieting.

evidence.note: The transcript uses HMAS Diamantina to explain machinery complexity, class repetition, inspector familiarity, and bearing faults.
A damaged computer illustrates how shock can propagate beyond the visibly affected component.
Rafting is described as vibration isolation that must remain flexible to provide quieting and survivability.

segments.summary: HMAS Diamantina, computer shock damage, and machinery rafting illustrate why bearings, electronics, mounts, and quieting systems must be tested as fitted.

segments.title: Stability calibration and weapons fit
segments.body: Modern opponents try to exploit low-probability failures, so weapons need more than nominal compatibility with a hull. A stabilized gun can lag behind a lively small ship or overcompensate on a large ship that proves steadier than expected. Either mismatch degrades the precision the fire-control system is intended to deliver. Older vertical-launch systems and missiles could likewise encounter problems on ships with unsuitable stability profiles. Trials measure the actual motion and vibration of the completed vessel, allowing calibration changes or, in harder cases, changes to where and on which ships a weapon can be fitted.

evidence.note: Undercompensation on lively ships and overcompensation when a ship proves more stable than predicted.
Older vertical-launch and missile fits illustrate how stability trials can change equipment placement and ship-system compatibility.

segments.summary: Gun stabilization and early vertical-launch examples show how the real motion of a completed hull can overturn paper assumptions about a weapon fit.

segments.title: Type 45 shore integration facilities
segments.body: The Type 45 program used large shore facilities, including integration testing on the Isle of Wight, to check SAMPSON radar with the rest of the combat system. A land installation can be turned off, modified in hardware or software, restarted, and run for long periods without tying up an operational destroyer. Human figures beside the radar make clear that its compact appearance on the ship disguises a substantial piece of equipment. These powerful shore radars could contribute to a wider UK defence network, although their testing role limits their availability. Experimental equipment and software require frequent shutdowns and alterations, so the installation cannot simply be treated as a continuously available operational radar. Passing the shore test still requires confirmation after installation in the ship's own structure and electronic environment. The same facility remains useful for later upgrades and integration work across the class.

evidence.note: The transcript describes Type 45 SAMPSON shore facilities, the radar's physical scale, repeated modification, and long-duration testing.
A proposed wider UK defence-network use for shore radars is qualified by the frequent shutdowns and experimental changes required by testing.
Land and barge testing are followed by renewed integration checks aboard ship, while shore facilities remain available for upgrades.

segments.summary: The Type 45's SAMPSON test installations show how a navy can repeatedly integrate, modify, and endurance-test a combat system ashore before proving it again aboard ship.

segments.title: Radar interference and electronic shielding
segments.body: Radar theory predated World War II, but wartime installation at scale exposed interactions that designers had little experience managing. Surface-search and air-search sets could degrade each other's performance or create false returns when placed too close together despite operating on different frequencies. Early remedies included greater physical separation, shielding, and changes in frequencies or equipment combinations. These lessons help explain why particular sets appeared on some ships or larger hulls but not on others. Modern land facilities can test a radar with its intended combat system, yet fitting it to the actual ship still requires another integration check.

evidence.note: The transcript distinguishes the long development of radar theory from its rapid wartime implementation.
Surface- and air-search sets are described as interfering or creating false positives until separation, shielding, or frequency changes were applied.
Modern land or sea test facilities cannot remove the need to synchronize and retest equipment after final shipboard installation.

segments.summary: World War II radar interference explains why set placement, shielding, frequencies, and final shipboard integration all have to be tested rather than assumed.

segments.title: Test infrastructure, class size, and readiness
segments.body: Shore integration facilities are expensive program assets that support multiple ships. The Type 45 program was planned around twelve hulls, and the quoted £6 billion program cost included these facilities. Describing the result as billion-pound destroyers obscures infrastructure that can be reused for successive ships and later upgrades. A large navy may accept testing more equipment aboard successive ships because a delay to one or two hulls is easier to absorb. A small navy has fewer substitutes, so it has a stronger reason to complete extensive land testing and deliver each ship ready to operate from the start.

evidence.note: The transcript links Type 45 shore facilities to a twelve-hull program, reusable infrastructure, upgrade work, and program cost.
Large and small navies are contrasted by their ability to absorb delayed ships and their incentive for pre-service testing.

segments.summary: The economics of the Type 45 test program show why one-time facilities, planned class size, and a navy's tolerance for delayed ships shape the trial strategy.

segments.title: Gunfire-induced weapons and electronics failures
segments.body: An unnamed navy, explicitly identified as neither British nor American, discovered that main-gun fire aboard cruisers built in the 1920s and 1930s could trigger prepared torpedo launchers. Launch charges were already loaded for the next test because the navy was trying to save money by scheduling gun and torpedo trials close together. Vibration or concussion from the gunfire appears to have triggered those charges, although the precise mechanism is uncertain. The accidental discovery reproduced a combat configuration that separate trials might have missed, and the fault required a manageable fix. As postwar radars became more sensitive, repeated heavy-gun salvos could knock delicate instruments slightly out of alignment without destroying the set outright. This could delay adoption of more sensitive radars on cruisers until protection against their own gunfire had been developed. Demonstrating these effects gave designers evidence for shock protection and funding authorities a concrete reason to pay for it.

evidence.note: An unnamed navy other than Britain or America discovers loaded torpedo-launch charges firing during cruiser gunnery trials, with uncertainty about vibration versus concussion as the mechanism.
Repeated heavy-gun salvos disturb sensitive postwar radar instruments, delaying some cruiser installations and establishing a need for shock hardening.

segments.summary: An interwar cruiser that launched torpedoes when its guns fired, followed by postwar radar alignment failures, demonstrates the value of testing systems together under realistic shock.

segments.title: Iowa gun shock and missile fits
segments.body: A weapon can be incompatible with a ship because of the shock produced by another weapon already aboard. The Iowa class illustrates why proposals for Aegis or a vertical-launch-system conversion involve protecting electronics and launch equipment from the battleship's own 16-inch gunfire. Hardening Aegis against such gunfire had not been a development priority. Later proposals therefore faced doubts about whether the conversion was sensible. The class carried Tomahawk missiles in canister launchers, where localized shock protection was more practical. Gun shock also helps explain the distribution of equipment around the ship.

evidence.note: Iowa-class equipment distribution and Aegis development priorities are connected to shock from the ship's own 16-inch guns.
Later upgrade proposals face doubts, while canister missile installations allow more practical shock protection than a VLS fit.

segments.summary: The Iowa class shows how the blast and shock of a ship's own 16-inch guns constrain radar, vertical-launch, and missile-upgrade choices.

segments.title: Weapons testing after Jutland
segments.body: A weapon must fire reliably, and its ammunition must produce the intended effect on the target. More realistic prewar armor-penetration testing probably would have exposed weaknesses in British shells before the Battle of Jutland and accelerated the development of improved ammunition. The gap between hits achieved and shells that performed properly materially limited British results in the battle. Jutland then left the Royal Navy with two lasting preoccupations: the German fleet's escape during the night and the reliability of weapons, shells, and torpedoes. The German escape also raised the fear that the enemy could have used the same freedom of movement to attack the British fleet at night. By World War II this experience encouraged extensive proof of weapon systems, a practice that remains necessary whenever missiles, ammunition, or their host ships are upgraded. Lives, ships, and potentially national survival depend on finding failures before combat.

evidence.note: The transcript links insufficient armor-penetration testing, British shell performance, and the results achieved at Jutland.
Jutland is said to produce Royal Navy preoccupations with night fighting and proof of shells, torpedoes, and other weapons.
Ongoing testing is tied to weapon upgrades, procurement decisions, crew lives, ship survival, and national risk.

segments.summary: Poor shell performance and the German fleet's escape at Jutland encouraged separate Royal Navy efforts to improve weapons proof and night fighting.

segments.title: Full-ship shock trials expose structural weak points
segments.body: A full-ship shock trial pushes equipment close to failure to identify weak points while limiting expensive damage. The way shock travels through the real structure can produce surprises. A door opening may require a strong point that transmits the load toward a pane of glass differently than expected. Glass rated for shock resistance can then break despite its apparent suitability on paper. Testing the installed structure reveals these interactions between individually acceptable components.

evidence.note: Shock trials seek breaking points, with resistant glass failing because a door and structural reinforcement change how shock reaches it.

segments.summary: Shock-resistant glass can still break when nearby doors and reinforcements change how a load travels through the completed ship.

segments.title: Computer shock models need physical trial data
segments.body: Navies have a financial and scheduling incentive to substitute computer models for physical shock trials. A real trial can damage a new vessel, delay service, require repairs, and in a severe failure risk losing the ship. A possible approach is to shock-test the first ship in a class, or the second if the first is urgently needed, then use the resulting data to inform computer checks of later ships. This still requires physical evidence to establish whether the design assumptions hold. That evidence may also support crew confidence and gives funders proof of the shock resistance claimed for an expensive vessel.

evidence.note: Computer-only testing avoids damage, repairs, delay, and the risk of losing a ship but cannot provide the required physical proof.
A possible first- or second-in-class trial could inform modeling of later ships, with hard data needed for design proof and funding accountability and potentially crew confidence.

segments.summary: Testing an early ship could provide the measured data needed to assess later ships by computer, while avoiding reliance on unproved shock-resistance claims.

segments.title: Commissioning crews write the operating manual
segments.body: Contractors and test teams supply technical documents, but the first-in-class crew turns them into an operating manual grounded in experience aboard the real ship. The commissioning captain is often more senior and experienced than later commanding officers because that officer must oversee both the crew and a multi-author body of knowledge. Experienced crew members combine contractor documents, trial results, and their own operating experience into standard procedures. These decisions also help establish the ship's working culture and traditions. HMS Queen Elizabeth's commissioning captain illustrates the judgment expected in this role: the captain must know the crew well enough to assess the information each contributor supplies. The resulting manual guides how the ship will be operated throughout its service.

evidence.note: An experienced first crew and captain combine contractor documents, trial results, and operating experience into the ship manual, procedures, and culture.
Queen Elizabeth's commissioning captain illustrates the seniority, knowledge of the crew, and editorial judgment needed to assess their contributions.

segments.summary: The first crew combines contractor documents, trial results, and operating experience into the procedures and working culture that guide the ship's service.

segments.title: Major refits require revised operating manuals
segments.body: An operating manual accumulates amendments as equipment changes during a ship's service. A major refit that replaces engines, generators, control systems, or radars can require a substantial new edition while retaining useful parts of the earlier manual. Officers selected for this work may be more senior or bring experience from serving aboard the ship before its modernization. Familiarity with the old procedures helps them recognize what must change when the revised systems enter operation. Navies need a personnel pool that includes capable operators who can also document technical work clearly.

evidence.note: Routine amendments give way to a substantial new manual edition after a major refit changes multiple systems.
Previous service aboard the ship and the ability to document technical work affect selection of officers and other personnel.

segments.summary: Replacing machinery, controls, or radars requires experienced crews to revise the procedures developed for the ship's earlier configuration.

segments.title: Fleet exercises reveal integration problems
segments.body: A warship that works by itself still has to integrate with destroyers, frigates, allied ships, and replenishment vessels. Fleet exercises can reveal too few communications positions for the traffic that must pass between ships and aircraft. A layout that places several vocal operators close together can also create enough overlapping speech to cause confusion even when they wear headphones. Data links reduce some spoken traffic, but command-space acoustics and human coordination still matter. Positions that regularly require speech can be interspersed with quieter stations, or with operators who usually speak at different times, so simultaneous calls are easier to hear.

evidence.note: Exercises with escorts, allies, and auxiliaries expose insufficient communications positions or interference from operators speaking close together.
Data sharing reduces voice traffic, while interspersing vocal stations with quieter positions helps crews hear spoken calls.

segments.summary: Exercises with escorts, allies, and auxiliaries test communications capacity and reveal whether closely grouped operators can hear one another clearly.

segments.title: Embarked air groups test carrier support capacity
segments.body: An aircraft carrier must integrate its own systems with the complex systems of the aircraft operating from it. Embarked squadrons also bring aircrew, aircraft engineers, and support personnel who use the ship's hangars, magazines, accommodation, and catering spaces. Their arrival can expose difficulties that were absent when the ship operated with its own crew alone. Toilets, showers, and waste management must cope with the enlarged population as well as the demands of flying operations. The curry-night example illustrates why calculated capacity still needs to be tested against actual use.

evidence.note: Aircraft and squadron personnel introduce further systems, space requirements, and sanitation demands aboard a carrier.
The curry-night example contrasts calculated toilet, shower, and waste capacity with experience of actual operating loads.

segments.summary: Aircraft operations bring additional personnel and equipment aboard, putting hangars, magazines, catering, sanitation, and waste systems under their intended operating load.

segments.title: A French Navy moving shock trial
segments.body: French Navy footage shows a crewed ship absorbing a nearby explosion during a shock trial. The ship appears to be moving slowly past a large charge, introducing some of the variation in shock effects discussed earlier. Screens have added tape as a precaution against breakage. After the detonation, some computers shut down and need resetting while others remain in operation, and the lights return quickly. The near miss still transmits visible force through the vessel, showing why trials inspect both immediate damage and the ability of essential systems to recover. A final clip shows an older ship's back broken by a torpedo exploding beneath the keel.

evidence.note: The transcript introduces French Navy full-shock-trial footage and observes that the ship moves slowly past the charge.
The reaction notes a crew aboard, taped screens, computers that shut down or stay working, rapid lighting recovery, and visible near-miss shock effects.
The final footage shows an older ship whose back is broken by an under-keel torpedo detonation.

segments.summary: French Navy footage shows shipboard systems reacting to a near-miss explosion, followed by an under-keel torpedo detonation against an older ship.
